The addition of Igbogun and Oke-Eri communities is based on their geographic isolation and lack of alternative health facilities within a 10-kilometre radius. Baseline data from the assessment indicates that only 23% of women in these communities have received at least one antenatal care visit, compared to the LGA average of 61%. LRI has already conducted a preliminary community engagement in both communities, and the traditional leadership has expressed willingness to host outreach sessions. No additional vehicles are required for this expansion, as the existing mobile health units can be re-routed to cover the new communities on alternating weeks.

This change aligns with the LSPHCB 2023 Annual Operational Plan priority to increase immunisation coverage in underserved communities and reduce maternal mortality in rural wards.

SECTION B — JUSTIFICATION

B.1 Background

The contract was originally awarded for the period 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2023. Under CR 03-2023, the service scope was expanded to include six additional outreach sessions per LGA in Epe and Ikorodu, and two new communities were added. The additional funding of ₦4,950,000 for this expansion was approved, and the budget table in CR 03-2023 reflects the revised quarterly allocations.

B.2 Why the Extension Is Necessary

The delay in approval of CR 03-2023, combined with seasonal factors affecting community participation, has made it impossible to deliver the full agreed number of sessions by the original contract end date. The outstanding sessions are not optional; they are required to meet the programme's output targets and to ensure that the outcome evaluation for the two new communities is based on a complete cycle of interventions.

B.3 Community Impact

If the extension is not granted, the following consequences are anticipated:

- The two new communities (Badore and Ibeshe) will have received only 60% of the planned outreach sessions, undermining the programme's objective of establishing sustained health-seeking behaviour.
- The outcome report for the expanded scope will be incomplete, and the LSPHCB will not have the data needed to decide on a possible scale-up in 2024.
- Community trust in the programme will be damaged, as several session dates have already been announced publicly and postponed once.

B.4 Alternative Options Considered

1. Compressing the remaining sessions into November–December 2023: Rejected. This would require running two sessions per week in each LGA, which is not feasible given the availability of community venues, the need for a minimum two-week gap between sessions for behaviour-reinforcement messaging, and the capacity of the LRI field team.
2. Reducing the number of sessions: Rejected. This would constitute a reduction in service scope and would require a separate change request, and it would undermine the programme's outcome targets.
3. Transferring the outstanding sessions to a different implementing partner: Rejected. This would require a new procurement process and would likely cost more than the remaining budget, and it would disrupt community relationships.

This Change Request seeks approval for the following modifications to the approved work plan and budget for the Community Health Outreach Program:

### C. Reason for Change

The original project design assumed a single training cohort of 40 volunteers. During Phase 1 implementation, the following factors emerged:

- The target communities are spread across five local government areas with significant travel distances. A single training venue required volunteers from distant LGAs to travel long distances or stay overnight, which was not feasible for many participants.
- Attendance data from the Phase 1 orientation sessions showed that volunteers are more likely to complete training when sessions are shorter and held closer to their home communities.
- The LSPHCB monitoring team, during its September site visit, recommended that training be delivered in smaller batches to improve retention and practical skill demonstration.
- Two additional outreach posts were created in late September to serve newly identified settlements. These posts require an additional 10 volunteers (total 50) to operate effectively.

The proposed changes are intended to strengthen the quality of training and ensure adequate volunteer coverage across all outreach posts.

SECTION B — JUSTIFICATION

B.1 Background

The contract was originally awarded for the period 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2023. Under CR 03-2023, the service scope was expanded to include six additional outreach sessions per LGA in Epe and Ikorodu, and two new communities were added. The additional funding of ₦4,950,000 for this expansion was approved, and the budget table in CR 03-2023 reflects the revised quarterly allocations.

B.2 Why the Extension Is Necessary

The delay in approval of CR 03-2023, combined with seasonal factors affecting community participation, has made it impossible to deliver the full agreed number of sessions by the original contract end date. The outstanding sessions are not optional; they are required to meet the programme's output targets and to ensure that the outcome evaluation for the two new communities is based on a complete cycle of interventions.

B.3 Community Impact

If the extension is not granted, the following consequences are anticipated:

- The two new communities (Badore and Ibeshe) will have received only 60% of the planned outreach sessions, undermining the programme's objective of establishing sustained health-seeking behaviour.
- The outcome report for the expanded scope will be incomplete, and the LSPHCB will not have the data needed to decide on a possible scale-up in 2024.
- Community trust in the programme will be damaged, as several session dates have already been announced publicly and postponed once.

B.4 Alternative Options Considered

1. Compressing the remaining sessions into November–December 2023: Rejected. This would require running two sessions per week in each LGA, which is not feasible given the availability of community venues, the need for a minimum two-week gap between sessions for behaviour-reinforcement messaging, and the capacity of the LRI field team.
2. Reducing the number of sessions: Rejected. This would constitute a reduction in service scope and would require a separate change request, and it would undermine the programme's outcome targets.
3. Transferring the outstanding sessions to a different implementing partner: Rejected. This would require a new procurement process and would likely cost more than the remaining budget, and it would disrupt community relationships.

### B. Summary of Request

This Change Request seeks approval for the following modifications to the approved work plan and budget for the Community Health Outreach Program:

1. **Revised Volunteer Training Schedule** – Replacing the single five-day training session for 40 volunteers with two three-day sessions for 25 volunteers each, to improve learning outcomes and reduce volunteer fatigue.
2. **Increased Volunteer Cohort** – Increasing the number of trained volunteers from 40 to 50 to cover the additional outreach posts created during Phase 1.
3. **Budget Adjustments** – An overall increase of NGN 1,150,000 (2.1% of the original approved budget) to cover additional training venue hire, per diem adjustments, and increased volunteer stipends.

A full narrative justification, revised work plan, and budget impact summary are provided in Sections E, F, and G below.

---

### C. Reason for Change

The original project design assumed a single training cohort of 40 volunteers. During Phase 1 implementation, the following factors emerged:

- The target communities are spread across five local government areas with significant travel distances. A single training venue required volunteers from distant LGAs to travel long distances or stay overnight, which was not feasible for many participants.
- Attendance data from the Phase 1 orientation sessions showed that volunteers are more likely to complete training when sessions are shorter and held closer to their home communities.
- The LSPHCB monitoring team, during its September site visit, recommended that training be delivered in smaller batches to improve retention and practical skill demonstration.
- Two additional outreach posts were created in late September to serve newly identified settlements. These posts require an additional 10 volunteers (total 50) to operate effectively.

The proposed changes are intended to strengthen the quality of training and ensure adequate volunteer coverage across all outreach posts.

---

### D. Impact on Scope, Timeline, and Budget

| Aspect | Impact |
|---|---|
| Scope | No change to the overall project objectives or expected outputs. The number of training days increases from 5 to 6, and the volunteer cohort increases from 40 to 50. |
| Timeline | Training completion moves from 10 November to 17 November. Final report submission remains 31 December. All other milestones are adjusted as shown in Section F. |
| Budget | Increase of NGN 1,150,000 (from NGN 36,000,000 to NGN 37,150,000). Details in Section G. |

No change is requested to the project’s monitoring and evaluation framework, data collection tools, or reporting requirements.

---

### E. Justification Narrative

#### E.1 Training Delivery Model

The original training plan was designed for a single session of 40 volunteers over five days at one venue in Ikeja. Transportation analysis conducted during the August mobilisation phase showed that volunteers from Badagry and Epe would spend three to four hours each way to attend, and several indicated they would be unable to commit to a full week away from their primary livelihoods.
